summary: The page outlines business risks from government-mandated price reductions and access restrictions; legal and environmental claims, litigation outcomes and reserves, and tax disputes; changing laws, policies, tariffs and global minimum-tax rules; patent application and extension delays, intellectual-property challenges and limits on enforcement; IT outages, cyberattacks, theft, disruption and security threats; and risks from AI-enabled software and emerging technologies.

title: ABOUT PFIZER
summary: Pfizer is a Delaware-incorporated global biopharmaceutical company that discovers, develops, manufactures, markets, sells and distributes products worldwide, working across developed and emerging markets and collaborating to improve access to reliable, affordable healthcare. Most revenue comes from product sales; Pfizer emphasizes the health and economic value of medicines and vaccines, patient access, and engagement with patients, providers and payors on outcomes, pricing and contracting. Its purpose is “Breakthroughs that change patients’ lives,” guided by five principles: trust, science, innovation, time and execution. Its 2025 priorities are sharper R&D productivity, greater margins and efficiency, commercial excellence in key categories, and optimized capital allocation. Growth efforts focus on advancing its pipeline, maximizing existing products, and pursuing strategic business-development opportunities informed by ongoing portfolio reviews; further details are referenced in MD&A and Note 2.

title: COMMERCIAL OPERATIONS
summary: Pfizer manages operations through Biopharma, PC1 (contract development, manufacturing and specialty ingredients), and Pfizer Ignite (R&D services for selected biotech companies); only Biopharma is reportable. Commercial teams market and distribute products, while global functions handle research, development, manufacturing and supply. The 2024 Biopharma structure comprised Oncology, U.S. Commercial and International Commercial divisions. In 2025, Oncology activities were redistributed: U.S. Oncology commercial and global Oncology marketing joined U.S. Commercial, while Oncology medical affairs moved to global R&D. The 2025 U.S. division covers U.S. commercial and medical affairs, access/value and marketing, with Primary Care, Specialty Care and Oncology portfolios; International covers commercial and medical affairs outside the U.S. The text lists representative products in each therapeutic area and directs readers to Note 17, MD&A and risk factors for segment, revenue-driver and product-concentration information.

title: RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
key_items: Our R&D Priorities and Strategy; Our R&D Operations; Our R&D Pipeline
summary: R&D supports Pfizer’s mission by developing new medicines and vaccines and improving existing products. Priorities are differentiated therapies, stronger long-term capabilities, and flexible partnerships; focus areas include oncology, internal medicine, vaccines, and inflammation/immunology. Pfizer combines internal research with external collaborations, licenses, acquisitions, and investments. In 2024, oncology and other R&D operated separately; they merged on January 1, 2025, with potential efficiencies reinvested in research. The Portfolio Management Team allocates resources company-wide, so spending is not reported by phase or area. Drug development can exceed ten years and is costly and uncertain; pipeline, product-development, expense, collaboration, and risk details are referenced elsewhere.

title: COLLABORATION AND CO-PROMOTION AGREEMENTS
summary: Pfizer describes collaborations and co-promotion arrangements supporting development, R&D, sales and distribution. It outlines shared costs, profits, losses, royalties, commercialization rights and regional responsibilities for Comirnaty (BioNTech), Eliquis (BMS), Xtandi and Padcev (Astellas), Orgovyx (SMPS; combination-tablet collaboration terminated in December 2024), and Adcetris (Takeda), including applicable approvals and markets. Other product and pipeline collaborations also exist. Related revenues are generally reported as Alliance revenues, with specified exceptions for direct sales and most Comirnaty and Padcev revenue; further details are cited in the Business, Risk Factors and financial-statement sections.

title: INTERNATIONAL OPERATIONS
summary: The company operates globally, supplying medicines and vaccines to about 200 countries and territories. Emerging-market urbanization and middle-class growth offer opportunities and shape its strategy. Non-U.S. revenues were $24.9 billion (39% of total) in 2024, $31.4 billion (53%) in 2023, and $57.9 billion (57%) in 2022; revenues exceeded $500 million in 11, 14, and 24 countries, respectively, with the 2024 decline largely due to lower Comirnaty and Paxlovid sales. China was the largest non-U.S. market in 2024; Japan led in 2023 and 2022. Geographic details are in MD&A and Note 17B. International operations face country-specific risks, including global-operational and regulatory or pricing risks.

title: SALES AND MARKETING
summary: Pfizer sells prescription biopharmaceuticals and vaccines through wholesalers, healthcare providers, pharmacies, governments, and institutions; some government vaccine contracts can be renegotiated or terminated. It seeks preferred formulary access through rebates and collaborates with payors on disease-management education. Marketing, conducted in compliance with applicable laws, informs healthcare providers, patients, insurers, employers, and government agencies about approved uses, benefits, and risks; direct-to-consumer and public health advertising also promotes disease awareness, prevention, wellness, and patient assistance. Pfizer uses virtual and in-person customer engagement and reports generally positive responses to both.

title: PATENTS AND OTHER INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS
summary: Pfizer describes its patent, co-promotion and licensing rights for products, noting that patent duration and protection vary by country, extensions may compensate for regulatory or administrative delays, and regulatory exclusivity may overlap with patents. A table lists estimated U.S., European and Japanese basic-patent expirations for key products, with caveats and detailed notes on pending extensions, litigation, collaborations, territorial rights, royalties and market-specific status. Loss or invalidation of rights, settlements, or expiring licenses can trigger lower-priced generic or biosimilar competition and materially reduce revenue; impacts are expected to be moderate in 2025 and greater in 2026–2030. Pfizer defends its rights while considering patient access. Trademarks and trade dress are protected through renewable registrations or use-based rights.

title: COMPETITION
summary: The text describes intense competition in regulated markets across efficacy, safety, usability and cost, from global and smaller biopharma firms, generics and biosimilars, including patent challenges and rival R&D that can erode sales or make products obsolete. Pfizer responds through major R&D and business-development investment, continued research, product education, effective launches, organizational adaptation, ethical marketing and access programs, including Accord for a Healthier World. It notes vaccine competition from alternative and next-generation products; biosimilar competition and the value of early entry; and generic price, substitution and market pressures, including China’s QCE and VBP programs. It also explains how biosimilars are defined and regulated in the U.S. and EU.

title: PRICING PRESSURES AND MANAGED CARE ORGANIZATIONS
summary: The text describes commercial pricing pressures from cost-focused employers, high-deductible plans, utilization controls, insurer and PBM bargaining, and provider purchasing demands, which can reduce prices, reimbursement, coverage and product demand. Pfizer advocates for affordable access, engages payors and policymakers, assesses its market approach, and works with health authorities and payors to demonstrate product value. It also explains how growing, consolidating MCOs and PBMs use formularies, protocols, contracts and patient cost-sharing to control spending; favor preventive and cost-saving care; and restrict costly drugs. Formulary access depends on product value and competition, while higher-tier placement and cost controls threaten demand and financial performance.

title: RAW MATERIALS
summary: The company sources essential raw materials from numerous global suppliers; supplies have generally been sufficient, often with multiple sources available. It expects no significant availability-related operational impact in 2025 but is monitoring disruptions from geopolitical and trade negotiations that may affect costs. Mitigations include active supplier management, qualifying additional suppliers, and advance purchasing where possible.

title: GOVERNMENT REGULATION AND PRICE CONSTRAINTS

nodes.title: GOVERNMENT REGULATION AND PRICE CONSTRAINTS (intro)
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes extensive, costly global regulation of product approval, manufacturing, marketing, pricing, healthcare interactions, research, privacy, and reporting, with noncompliance risking penalties, business restrictions, and reputational harm. In the U.S., FDA and other agencies regulate drugs and biologics throughout development and marketing, including approval, trials, manufacturing, labeling, promotion, safety monitoring, supply-chain tracing, and emergency-use authorizations; biosimilars face reference-product exclusivity periods. Fraud-and-abuse laws govern marketing and healthcare-provider payments. Government programs require discounts, rebates, and price reporting. The IRA changes Medicare benefits and manufacturer discounts, imposes inflation rebates and government-set prices, and may reduce revenue: Eliquis pricing takes effect in 2026, Ibrance and Xtandi were selected for 2027, and further selections are possible. Legal challenges leave the program’s effects uncertain; Pfizer anticipates about $1 billion in unfavorable 2025 revenue impact from Part D redesign.

nodes.title: U.S. Biopharmaceutical Regulation and Marketing
nodes.summary: The FDA and other agencies regulate biopharmaceutical products throughout development and marketing, including clinical trials, safety and efficacy, manufacturing, labeling, promotion, distribution, surveillance, and reporting. Drug and biologic approval requires FDA review; obligations may include post-approval studies, adverse-event reporting, cGMPs, supply-chain tracing, and pharmacovigilance. Emergency Use Authorizations permit conditional use during declared emergencies while sponsors pursue full approval. Biosimilars face reference-product exclusivity periods: applications may be submitted after four years and approved after 12. Federal and state fraud-and-abuse, false-claims, disclosure, compliance, consumer-protection, and advertising laws govern marketing and financial interactions with healthcare providers.

nodes.title: Pricing, Reimbursement and Access Regulations
nodes.summary: The text reviews regulatory risks affecting Pfizer’s pricing, reimbursement and access, including required government discounts and price reporting; IRA Medicare benefit changes, manufacturer discounts, inflation rebates and negotiated prices, with Eliquis, Ibrance and Xtandi selected and an estimated $1 billion unfavorable 2025 revenue impact. It covers MDRP and 340B rule changes, litigation and contract-pharmacy policies; state Medicaid rebates and formulary controls; broader government and payer cost-containment pressures; anti-corruption laws; evolving privacy and cybersecurity obligations; and non-U.S. drug approval authorities and proposed EU pharmaceutical reforms.

nodes.title: Drug Pricing, Anti-Corruption and Data Privacy Risks
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from U.S. drug-pricing and reimbursement policies, including MDRP and 340B changes, litigation and enforcement over contract-pharmacy policies, state Medicaid rebates and formulary controls, and broader efforts to regulate prices and promote generics and biosimilars. It also outlines FCPA and similar anti-corruption requirements, and evolving privacy and data-security laws, cross-border compliance challenges, increased enforcement, and potential penalties, litigation and reputational harm from noncompliance or cybersecurity incidents.

nodes.title: New Drug Approvals
nodes.summary: The text outlines global pharmaceutical regulation, including marketing approvals in the EU, U.K., Japan, China and other markets, and a proposed EU legislation overhaul that could affect Pfizer. It describes pharmacovigilance oversight; government pricing and reimbursement controls, especially China’s VBP and other cost-containment measures; disclosure rules for healthcare-provider payments; global intellectual-property protections and challenges; evolving data-privacy obligations and risks; and environmental compliance and remediation spending. Pfizer reports 2024 environmental capital expenditures of $100 million and other environmental expenses of $174 million, with no material financial impact currently anticipated.

nodes.title: Pharmaceutical Regulation and Market Risks
nodes.summary: The text outlines EU and global pharmacovigilance oversight and growing regulation; government pricing and reimbursement controls, international access initiatives, and China’s cost-containment, negotiation, and VBP policies and their uncertain business impact. It covers disclosure requirements for transfers of value to healthcare providers; global patent protections, ongoing weaknesses and industry advocacy; and evolving, inconsistent privacy laws governing sensitive health data, with rising enforcement and risks of fines, litigation, and reputational harm.

summary: Pfizer faces extensive global regulation of drug development, approval, manufacturing, marketing, safety monitoring, distribution, privacy, reporting and environmental compliance; violations can bring penalties, restrictions and reputational harm. U.S. rules cover clinical trials, FDA approvals and emergency authorizations, post-market obligations, biosimilar exclusivity, healthcare-provider interactions and fraud, false-claims and disclosure laws. Pricing and access rules require discounts, rebates and reporting; the IRA changes Medicare benefits, imposes inflation rebates and negotiated prices, and may reduce revenue, including an estimated $1 billion adverse 2025 impact. MDRP, 340B, state Medicaid, payer controls and international measures such as China’s VBP add uncertainty. The section also covers global approval and pharmacovigilance, proposed EU reforms, anti-corruption requirements, intellectual-property protections, evolving privacy and cybersecurity risks, and environmental spending.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL MATTERS
summary: Pfizer complies with environmental laws and cleans up contamination from past industrial activity. In 2024, it spent $100 million on environmental capital expenditures and $174 million on other environmental expenses; it does not expect compliance costs to materially affect its capital expenditures or financial position. Pfizer’s 2040 net-zero goal targets 95% lower direct emissions and 90% lower value-chain emissions versus 2019, supported by an emissions-reduction plan involving technologies, climate solutions, and supplier targets. 2024 plan spending was not material; future costs and long-term impacts remain uncertain. Climate-related risks are discussed in the Risk Factors section.

title: OUR PEOPLE
key_items: Colleague Engagement; Performance and Leadership; Growth and Development
summary: Pfizer describes its 81,000-person global workforce and people-centered approach to attracting, developing, and retaining talent through supportive culture, merit-based opportunities, flexibility, and employee well-being. It covers leaders’ accountability and open communication; feedback channels, engagement surveys, and recognition; 2024 leadership attitudes, project-based work, and performance reviews; varied learning and career-growth paths; global environmental health and safety policies, training, and audits; extensive physical, mental, disability, financial, and workplace support programs; and annual public reporting on equitable pay based on role, education, experience, performance, and location.

title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS
summary: The section outlines material business risks alongside other SEC filings, while noting risks cannot all be predicted or identified and the list is not exhaustive. The company also faces general risks, including economic conditions, geopolitical events, extreme weather, and natural disasters. Known or unknown risks could materially harm operations, financial condition, results, cash flows, prospects, reputation, or credit ratings, now or in the future. The discussion includes forward-looking statements.

title: RISKS RELATED TO OUR BUSINESS, INDUSTRY AND OPERATIONS:

nodes.title: MANAGED CARE TRENDS
nodes.summary: Managed care organizations, PBMs and other payors have gained negotiating power through consolidation and increasingly use formularies, rebates, fees, deductibles, cost sharing and utilization controls to contain drug costs, especially for costly specialty medicines. Higher patient cost burdens may increase preference for generics. The company may not secure timely, adequate or favorable product pricing and formulary coverage. Payors also use market-entry blocks, exclusions, indication- or value-based pricing, and prior authorization or step therapy; further consolidation and public IRA prices may intensify pressure to favor cheaper alternatives or demand larger rebates. Related arrangements face substantial government scrutiny, and fraud-and-abuse safe harbors and guidance may change through legislation, regulation or court decisions.

nodes.title: COMPETITIVE PRODUCTS
nodes.summary: Pfizer warns that existing and emerging competitors—including branded, generic, at-risk generic, and biosimilar products—may reduce sales through better efficacy, safety, pricing, access, or other advantages; exclusivity expirations, patent challenges, and intense competition in China and vaccines add pressure. Revenue is concentrated in 11 products (66% in 2024) and significant customers, exposing results to product, market, safety, regulatory, supply, pricing, and customer risks; exclusivity losses are expected to have greater revenue impact in 2026–2030, while COVID-19 product revenues have declined or may fluctuate. Sustained growth depends on successful, reimbursed R&D, but high costs, regulatory and trial challenges, candidate failures, and poor investment or scientific choices may weaken the pipeline and returns.

nodes.title: Competition, Revenue Concentration, and R&D Risks
nodes.summary: The page describes generic and biosimilar competition, including early launches, patent challenges, pricing pressure, and access barriers; it notes expected revenue effects from exclusivity expirations, especially in 2026–2030. Revenue concentration in 11 products and major customers creates risks from product, market, legal, safety, supply, pricing, and customer changes; COVID-19 product revenues and Paxlovid use may fluctuate. It also explains the need to replenish the portfolio and the costs, regulatory, trial, scientific, investment, approval, and reimbursement uncertainties of R&D.

nodes.title: Global and Product Operations Risks
key_items: PRODUCT MANUFACTURING, SALES AND MARKETING RISKS
nodes.summary: Global operations face currency and interest-rate movements, economic and political instability, regulatory and trade changes, tariffs, public-health and climate-related disruptions, government pricing pressures, and emerging-market limitations. These risks may affect growth, payment and supply obligations, costs, revenues, assets, pensions, and financial guidance; international revenue exposure and related disclosures are noted. Manufacturing, supply, distribution, sales, and marketing may be disrupted by regulatory action, facility or supplier problems, recalls, shortages, disasters, or contract-manufacturer failures. Facility inspections and cGMP noncompliance can trigger enforcement and product impacts; nitrosamine monitoring may prompt market action, as illustrated by Chantix’s recall and potential return.

nodes.title: COLLABORATIONS AND OTHER RELATIONSHIPS WITH THIRD PARTIES
nodes.summary: Pfizer relies on third parties for research, development, manufacturing, commercialization, joint ventures, and outsourced services, often without controlling their activities; upfront transaction payments may hurt earnings or cash flow. Delays, failures, legal or regulatory noncompliance, disruptions, supply shortages, cyberattacks, labor issues, disasters, or damaged relationships could impair product development and supply, quality, timelines, data, compliance, and reputation. Expiration or termination of collaboration and co-promotion agreements may also reduce revenue.

nodes.title: COUNTERFEIT PRODUCTS
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s reputation and medicines make its products targets for counterfeiters. Counterfeits, often made in unsafe, unregulated conditions, threaten patient safety and could erode trust, reduce sales, trigger recalls, or lead to litigation. E-commerce, rogue online pharmacies, and deceptive retailer or social-media offers increase exposure; counterfeiters target high-demand products, with heightened attempts involving Pfizer’s internal medicine portfolio and COVID-19 treatments. Pfizer invests in education, detection technologies, supply monitoring and interdiction with law enforcement, and policy advocacy, but these efforts may not prevent counterfeit medicines from increasing.

summary: The section covers risks from payor consolidation and pricing, formulary and access controls, and scrutiny of rebate arrangements; competition, exclusivity losses, concentrated products and customers, fluctuating COVID-19 revenues, and uncertain, costly R&D; global economic, political, regulatory, trade, currency, pricing, and climate pressures; manufacturing, supply, quality, inspection, and recall disruptions; reliance on third parties and collaborations; and counterfeit medicines that threaten patient safety, reputation, and sales despite prevention efforts.

Drug development and approval face costly, uncertain trials, regulatory delays, safety and efficacy concerns, post-approval obligations, and possible withdrawal; Oxbryta was withdrawn, while Comirnaty has required studies. It also covers third-party patent disputes, infringement claims, launch delays, at-risk launches, and related costs and liabilities. IT and cybersecurity risks include system disruptions, data breaches, third-party and supply-chain vulnerabilities, sophisticated attacks, and potentially insufficient insurance. title: ITEM 1C. CYBERSECURITY
summary: Pfizer integrates cybersecurity into its NIST-aligned enterprise risk program, using threat monitoring, external collaboration, technical safeguards and testing, employee training and reporting, supplier oversight, incident-response plans, and cross-functional coordination. The Audit Committee oversees risk, receives CISO briefings and incident updates, while the CISO leads management’s program and response. Pfizer identifies diverse threats and potential asset, operational, and reputational harms, uses independent assessments to improve controls, and reported no known material cybersecurity incidents for 2024. Its properties include 251 global sites totaling about 37 million square feet, 37 PGS plants, U.S. R&D facilities of about 9 million square feet, and leased overseas labs; Pfizer considers its properties adequate. Legal proceedings are discussed in Note 16A.

It also describes product revenue deductions, presents deduction categories and annual amounts, explains the main 2024 increase drivers and favorable Paxlovid adjustment, and notes that deductions are estimated and influenced by sales volume, product mix, and contractual or statutory terms.

nodes.title: Total Revenues—Selected Product Discussion
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s 2024 Form 10-K reports regional and worldwide revenues and operational growth commentary for selected Biopharma products, including Eliquis, Prevnar, Paxlovid, Vyndaqel, Comirnaty, oncology and other medicines, plus Pfizer CentreOne. Explanations cover demand, market share, pricing, competition, launches, acquisitions, COVID-19 sales, and vaccination trends. The text also directs readers to patent, litigation and product-indication disclosures, and presents costs and expenses, highlighting lower cost of sales due mainly to the absence of 2023 COVID-19 inventory charges and favorable sales mix, partly offset by Seagen-related costs; it notes seasonal vaccine demand.

nodes.title: Costs and Expenses
key_items: Selllng, Informational and Administrative Expenses; Research and Development Expenses; Amortization of Intangible Assets; Other (Income)/Deductions––Net
Restructuring Charges and Other Costs Associated with Acquisitions and Cost-Reduction/Productivity Initiatives
Realigning our Cost Base Program; Manufacturing Optimization Program; Seagen acquisition
nodes.summary: The text reports Pfizer’s 2024 product and segment revenues and operational changes: Inlyta and Pfizer CentreOne declined, while Abrysvo fell amid lower U.S. older-adult vaccinations, partly offset by maternal and international demand; CentreOne’s decline reflected lower third-party manufacturing, partly offset by services. It summarizes 2024 expenses and year-over-year drivers, including cost-of-sales reductions, sales and R&D changes, and higher amortization. It describes cost-reduction, manufacturing optimization, and Seagen synergy targets, explains changes in other income/deductions for 2024 and 2023, and presents tax provisions and effective tax rates, with references to related notes and disclosures.

nodes.title: Provision/(Benefit) for Taxes on Income
nodes.summary: Selling, informational and administrative expenses fell $41 million, while R&D rose $143 million and intangible amortization increased $553 million, with drivers including Seagen, compensation, lower marketing, cost realignment and asset changes. Pfizer outlines savings and costs for its cost-base, manufacturing optimization and Seagen synergy programs, plus ongoing productivity and gross-margin priorities. Other deductions worsened $4.2 billion in 2024 versus 2023, but improved $840 million in 2023 versus 2022. The text reports tax provisions and effective rates, refers to Note 5 for details, and warns OECD Pillar Two rules effective from 2024 may materially increase tax expense.

Reviews Pfizer’s 2022–2024 revenues by geography and segment, explaining annual changes and selected product performance, including demand, competition, pricing, launches, acquisitions, COVID-19 trends, and foreign exchange. Reports product revenue deductions and their drivers, and discusses cost of sales and other expenses, including Seagen-related costs, R&D, amortization, cost reductions, manufacturing optimization, and synergy targets. Also covers other income and deductions, income tax provisions and effective rates, related disclosures, and potential tax impacts of OECD Pillar Two rules.

nodes.title: PRODUCT DEVELOPMENTS
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s development pipeline update, published February 4, 2025, is available online and lists research candidates, indications, development phases, and mechanisms of action for specified phases. The section describes significant FDA, EU, and Japanese regulatory actions and pending filings as of the filing date; its table covers recent filing and approval milestones and pending decisions, listing products including vaccines, medicines, and combinations. Filing dates mean FDA acceptance in the U.S. and EMA validation in the EU; footnote (a) notes geographic differences in approved indications.

summary: Explains the purpose and presentation of Pfizer’s MD&A, including recast royalty income and comparisons with prior filings. Reviews 2024 performance, business conditions, strategy, outlook, product and regional drivers, policy and market pressures, risks, and operational initiatives. Describes critical accounting policies, estimates, assumptions, and contingencies. Analyzes 2022–2024 revenue, deductions, expenses, taxes, and other income, including key drivers and tax developments. Summarizes pipeline information and significant regulatory filings, approvals, and pending decisions across major markets.

title: INDICATION OR PROPOSED INDICATION
summary: The text lists proposed or approved indications and U.S., EU, and Japan approval/filing dates for vaccines, migraine treatments, ulcerative colitis, cancers, hemophilia, and bacterial infections, including pneumococcal, tick-borne encephalitis, RSV, and COVID-19 prevention. It provides collaboration, trademark, and regional commercialization-rights notes; records the Penbraya EU authorization withdrawal, termination of Beqvez development and its license, and withdrawal of Ngenla’s EU filing for adult growth hormone deficiency; and introduces information on additional indications and late-stage drug candidates.

title: PRODUCT/CANDIDATE
summary: Pfizer’s late-stage pipeline lists candidates and target uses across oncology, hematology, vaccines, and other diseases, including additional indications and formulations for marketed products, with collaboration partners identified in footnotes. Pfizer terminated development of giroctocogene fitelparvovec and sisunatovir; its influenza/COVID-19 mRNA vaccine moved from Phase 3 back to Phase 1 after missing an immunogenicity objective. Pfizer withdrew Oxbryta, ended its trials and access programs, and is reviewing safety signals with regulators; the EMA suspended its authorization and the FDA placed its investigational application on hold. The FDA also partially suspended new enrollment in osivelotor studies. Further R&D and collaboration information is referenced elsewhere in the filing.

title: NON-GAAP FINANCIAL MEASURE: ADJUSTED INCOME

nodes.title: Definition
nodes.summary: Pfizer explains Adjusted income, its components, and Adjusted diluted EPS as non-GAAP measures management uses alongside GAAP results to assess recurring operations, compare performance year over year, forecast, and inform budgeting and compensation. The measures exclude amortization, certain acquisition-related items, discontinued operations, and significant items; definitions and comparable GAAP measures are identified. Adjusted diluted EPS and Adjusted net income inform incentive awards, subject to additional financial and nonfinancial factors. Pfizer cautions that these nonstandard measures have limited usefulness, may not compare across companies, omit some period events, and are not substitutes for GAAP measures. Performance management also uses R&D productivity and absolute and relative shareholder returns.

nodes.title: Adjusted Income and Adjusted Diluted EPS
nodes.summary: Adjusted income and diluted EPS exclude intangible-asset amortization, acquisition-related transaction, integration, restructuring, depreciation and purchase-accounting effects (without adjusting for synergies), discontinued operations and disposal gains or losses, and individually assessed significant or unusual items. These may include restructuring, impairments, equity-security gains or losses, pension remeasurements, legal matters, and other nonrecurring costs or gains; some may recur. The text explains the rationale and timing of these exclusions, notes discontinued-operation restatements do not affect related compensation measures, and presents GAAP-to-adjusted reconciliation headings and cost-of-sales figures for two periods, including non-GAAP tax adjustments; components may not sum to totals.

nodes.title: Year Ended December 31, 2024
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s 2022–2024 reconciliation presents GAAP reported and non-GAAP adjusted expenses, net income attributable to common shareholders, and diluted earnings per share, with adjustments for amortization, acquisitions, discontinued operations, restructuring, impairments, equity securities, pensions, other items, and taxes. Notes explain tax rates, immaterial R&D amounts, acquisition-cost breakdowns, restructuring scope, and significant other adjustments—including Haleon investment gains and costs, legal matters, a facility sale, divestitures and investment income, and 2023 tornado-related losses and insurance recoveries. Figures may not sum due to rounding.

summary: Pfizer defines Adjusted income and Adjusted diluted EPS as non-GAAP measures used with GAAP results to assess recurring performance, compare periods, forecast, budget and inform compensation, while noting their limitations and noncomparability. The section details excluded amortization, acquisition and restructuring costs, discontinued operations, and significant or unusual gains and losses; explains exclusion rationales and compensation treatment; and reconciles GAAP and adjusted expenses, net income and diluted EPS for 2022–2024. Notes cover tax effects, acquisition and restructuring items, legal matters, investment gains and losses, facility sales, divestitures, and disaster-related costs and recoveries; figures may not sum due to rounding.

title: ANALYSIS OF THE CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS
summary: The text compares Pfizer’s consolidated cash flows for 2024, 2023, and 2022 and explains 2024 versus 2023 changes. Operating cash provided rose to $12.744 billion, mainly due to higher adjusted net income, partly offset by ordinary-course receipt and payment timing, lower Comirnaty and Paxlovid advance payments, and inventory changes. Investing cash shifted to $2.652 billion provided, reflecting 2023 Seagen acquisition payments and 2024 Haleon sale proceeds, partly offset by increased short-term investment purchases. Financing used $17.140 billion, largely reflecting 2023 debt proceeds and greater 2024 short-term borrowing repayments.

title: ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION, LIQUIDITY, CAPITAL RESOURCES AND MARKET RISK
summary: Pfizer describes its liquidity and funding sources, emphasizing strong operating cash flow, working-capital management, conservative investments, cash and credit facilities, and capital-market access. It lists internal and external funding sources and reports high-quality Moody’s and S&P credit ratings, with a warning that ratings may change. Its capital framework prioritizes dividends, business reinvestment, then repurchases after deleveraging; it reports the declared 2025 dividend, unused repurchase authorization, and Haleon share sales and accounting changes. It outlines off-balance-sheet arrangements, indemnities, contingent milestone payments, and major obligations, including debt, taxes, commitments, capital spending, and leases. Hyperinflation exposure is immaterial. Market-risk discussion covers foreign exchange, interest rates, and equity prices; modeled impacts on net income from specified changes are not significant.

title: Accounting Standards and Market Risk
key_items: ITEM 7A. QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK
summary: The page references recently adopted accounting standards in Note 1B and describes two standards not yet adopted: enhanced income tax disclosures, effective for annual reports in 2025, and disaggregated expense and selling-expense disclosures, effective for annual reports in 2027 and interim reports in 2028. Early adoption is permitted for both, and each will increase financial statement note disclosures. Market-risk disclosures are incorporated by reference to the corresponding MD&A discussion.

title: ITEM 8. FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND SUPPLEMENTARY DATA

nodes.title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
key_items: Opinion on the Consolidated Financial Statements
Evaluation of the U.S. Medicare, Medicaid, and performance-based contract rebates accrual
Evaluation of gross unrecognized tax benefits
nodes.summary: The auditor gives an unqualified opinion that Pfizer’s 2022–2024 consolidated financial statements fairly present its financial position, results, and cash flows under U.S. GAAP, and notes a separate unqualified opinion on internal controls. The report explains management’s and auditor’s responsibilities, PCAOB standards, independence, and audit procedures. It identifies two critical audit matters: estimating U.S. Medicare, Medicaid, and performance-based rebates, and evaluating gross unrecognized tax benefits ($4.5 billion), describing related judgment, controls, and audit procedures.

nodes.title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
key_items: Evaluation of product liability and other product-related litigation
Evaluation of the fair value measurement of the developed technology rights and in-process research and development intangible assets acquired in the Seagen business combination
nodes.summary: The auditor describes procedures for evaluating Pfizer’s uncertain tax benefits, including tax-law and transfer-pricing assessments, settlements, limitation periods, and liability calculations. It identifies product-related litigation as a critical audit matter, detailing controls and procedures used to assess legal counsel information, litigation status, historical estimates, and industry data. It also identifies the fair value of Seagen-acquired technology rights and in-process research and development as a critical audit matter, outlining valuation controls, sensitivity analyses, assessments of revenue growth and technical/regulatory success assumptions, and specialist review of discount rates. The report notes the auditor’s service dates are known only to extend back at least to 1942, and is dated February 27, 2025, in New York.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statements of Operations
nodes.summary: Pfizer Inc.’s consolidated statements of operations for 2024, 2023, and 2022 report revenues by product, alliance, and royalties; operating costs and expenses; pretax income, taxes, continuing and discontinued operations, noncontrolling interests, and net income attributable to common shareholders. They also present basic and diluted earnings per share by continuing and discontinued operations, weighted-average shares, and references to related notes.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income
nodes.summary: Pfizer Inc.’s consolidated statements of comprehensive income for 2024, 2023, and 2022 report net income; other comprehensive income or loss before and after tax, including foreign-currency translation, derivative and available-for-sale security gains or losses, and benefit-plan adjustments; comprehensive income before noncontrolling interests; and amounts attributable to noncontrolling interests and Pfizer Inc. Footnotes identify where reclassification adjustments were recorded, and the statement refers readers to accompanying notes.

summary: Presents the independent auditor’s unqualified opinions on Pfizer’s 2022–2024 financial statements and internal controls, its responsibilities and procedures, and critical audit matters involving rebates, uncertain tax benefits, product litigation, and Seagen technology and in-process R&D valuations. Includes consolidated statements of operations and comprehensive income for 2022–2024, covering revenues, expenses, income, taxes, earnings per share, shares, other comprehensive income items, noncontrolling interests, and related notes.

title: Consolidated Balance Sheets
summary: Pfizer Inc.’s consolidated balance sheets as of December 31, 2024 and 2023, in millions except per-share data, list current and noncurrent assets, including cash, investments, receivables, inventories, property, intangibles, and goodwill; current and long-term liabilities, including borrowings, payables, debt, and benefit obligations; and commitments and contingencies. They also report common stock, paid-in capital, treasury stock, retained earnings, accumulated comprehensive loss, noncontrolling interests, total equity, and total liabilities and equity, with comparative figures and specified share and debt details.

title: Consolidated Statements of Equity
summary: Pfizer’s 2024 Form 10-K presents consolidated statements of equity and cash flows for 2022–2024, in millions. The equity statement tracks shareholder and noncontrolling interests, including net income, other comprehensive income or loss, dividends per share, stock issuance, share-based payments, share repurchases, and ending balances. Cash flows detail operating adjustments and working-capital changes; investing in property, securities, acquisitions, and Haleon/Consumer Healthcare transactions; financing through debt, repurchases, and dividends; exchange-rate effects and cash balances. Supplemental disclosures report cash taxes, interest, hedges, and lease assets, with notes references.

title: Note 1. Basis of Presentation and Significant Accounting Policies
key_items: A. Basis of Presentation; B. New Accounting Standards Adopted in 2024; C. Estimates and Assumptions; D. Acquisitions
B. New Accounting Standards Adopted in 2024
summary: Pfizer’s consolidated statements follow U.S. GAAP, include controlled subsidiaries, eliminate intercompany transactions, and use different year-ends for U.S. and foreign subsidiaries. It describes operating segments, the Seagen acquisition and other business activity, and 2024 reclassifications of royalty, segment, and geographic information. New standards adopted in 2024 had no financial impact or added segment disclosures. The note explains estimates’ broad use, uncertainty, risks, and regular reassessment, and acquisition accounting: fair-value recognition, expensed transaction costs, goodwill treatment, and contingent consideration.

title: Pfizer Inc.

nodes.title: Pfizer Inc. (intro)
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes its U.S. GAAP consolidation and segment structure, Seagen acquisition, prior-period reclassifications, and 2024 accounting standards adopted. It explains the use and uncertainty of estimates; acquisition accounting, including contingent consideration; fair-value methods, input levels, valuation techniques, and review controls; foreign-currency translation; and revenue recognition, sales contracts, and deductions from product revenue, including control-transfer and bill-and-hold criteria.

nodes.title: Fair Value and Foreign Currency Translation
nodes.summary: Describes fair value measurement using an exit-price perspective, valuation approaches (income, market, and cost), and the Level 1–3 input hierarchy. It outlines techniques and inputs for valuing securities, derivatives, and money market funds, plus reviews of third-party pricing. It also explains contingent-consideration remeasurement and foreign-currency translation for international and highly inflationary operations, including where resulting gains and losses are recorded.

nodes.title: G. Revenues and Trade Accounts Receivable
nodes.summary: The text explains Pfizer’s revenue recognition, including shipment, delivery, control indicators, and bill-and-hold criteria; sales contracts, returns, incentives, and estimates for rebates, chargebacks, discounts, and allowances across U.S. and international markets; customer channels, product seasonality, revenue concentration, patent-loss effects, and related accrual balances. It describes receivable valuation and credit-loss reserves. It also covers accounting for collaboration revenue, costs, milestones, and royalties; inventory valuation; selling and advertising, R&D, and acquired in-process R&D expenses; and the initial accounting policy for property, plant, and equipment.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies for Revenue, Expenses, and Inventories
key_items: I. Cost of Sales and Inventories
J. Selllng, Informational and Administrative Expenses; K. Research and Development Expenses; L. Acquired In-Process Research and Development Expenses
J. Selllng, Informational and Administrative Expenses
L. Acquired In-Process Research and Development Expenses
nodes.summary: The page describes receivables credit-loss estimates, monitoring, write-offs, and immaterial allowance activity in 2024 and 2023. It explains collaboration accounting for revenues, costs, reimbursements, milestones, and royalties; inventory valuation and classification; expensing and advertising costs; R&D expense recognition; and the accounting and amortization of acquired in-process R&D payments before and after regulatory approval.

nodes.title: M. Long-Lived Assets
nodes.summary: The text outlines Pfizer’s accounting policies for long-lived assets: recording and depreciating property and equipment, amortizing finite-lived intangibles, and not amortizing goodwill or indefinite-lived intangibles; it also describes impairment reviews and testing methods for each asset type. It explains restructuring and acquisition-related costs, including employee, facility, integration, and transaction costs and their accounting. Cash-equivalent definitions and cash-flow classifications for hedging instruments are provided, along with measurement and reporting rules for public equities, available-for-sale and held-to-maturity debt, and certain private equity investments.

nodes.title: Asset Impairment, Restructuring, and Cash Flow Policies
key_items: N. Restructuring Charges and Other Costs Associated with Acquisitions and Cost-Reduction/Productivity Initiatives
O. Cash Equivalents and Statement of Cash Flows
nodes.summary: The page explains depreciation and amortization of tangible and intangible assets, goodwill accounting, and impairment testing for finite- and indefinite-lived assets and reporting units. It describes acquisition-related and cost-reduction restructuring costs, their classification and recognition, and potential effects across business functions. It defines cash equivalents and explains how cash flows from hedging instruments are classified in the statement of cash flows.

nodes.title: P. Investments and Derivative Financial Instruments
nodes.summary: Investment classification depends on investment type, intent and ability to hold, and level of influence. Public equity and available-for-sale debt are measured at fair value, with changes recognized in earnings or other comprehensive income, respectively; held-to-maturity debt is at amortized cost; certain private equity is measured at cost adjusted for impairment and observable price changes. Significant-influence investments use the equity method, including recognition of the investor’s income share and allocation of acquisition excess. Realized gains and losses use specific identification. Financial assets are regularly assessed for impairment; equity-method impairments require an other-than-temporary decline. Derivatives are carried at fair value, with changes recognized in earnings or, for qualifying hedges, other comprehensive income.

nodes.title: Q. Tax Assets and Liabilities and Income Tax Contingencies
nodes.summary: The text explains accounting for current tax assets, including intercompany inventory tax effects and recoverable tax receivables; deferred tax assets and liabilities, valuation allowances, net presentation, and the election to recognize deferred taxes on future GILTI; and other noncurrent tax assets arising from cross-jurisdiction tax relief. It describes other tax payables, including uncertain positions and the repatriation tax liability. It also outlines the recognition, measurement, reassessment, classification, and interest and penalty treatment of income tax contingencies, noting that estimates and outcomes may differ materially.

nodes.title: R. Pension and Postretirement Benefit Plans
nodes.summary: Most worldwide employees participate in defined benefit and/or contribution pension plans. U.S. plans also include qualified and supplemental pensions and retiree medical benefits. Non-service benefit costs and immediately recognized actuarial remeasurement gains or losses are reported in Other (income)/deductions—net. Each defined benefit plan’s funded status is recorded as an asset or liability; obligations reflect actuarial present values based on assumptions including discount rates, investment returns, turnover, mortality, future compensation, medical costs, and cost-sharing. Plan assets are measured at fair value.

nodes.title: S. Legal and Environmental Contingencies
nodes.summary: The company and certain subsidiaries face ordinary-course contingencies, including patent, product liability and other litigation, commercial matters, environmental claims, government investigations, guarantees, and indemnifications. Accruals are recorded when losses are probable and reasonably estimable; for a loss range, the best estimate is accrued, or the lowest amount if none is better. Expected insurance recoveries are recorded when assured.

nodes.title: T. Share-Based Payments
A. Acquisitions
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes its share-based compensation accounting, then details acquisitions. Seagen’s 2023 purchase terms, strategic rationale, finalized purchase-price allocation and measurement adjustments, acquired contingencies and tax liabilities, goodwill, reported post-acquisition results, and unaudited 2022–23 pro forma results and adjustments are presented. The text also summarizes 2022 acquisitions of GBT, Biohaven, Arena, and ReViral, including consideration, assets and liabilities recognized, compensation or R&D charges, transaction structure, and whether pro forma information was provided.

nodes.title: B. Divestitures
key_items: Divestiture of Early-Stage Rare Disease Gene Therapy Portfolio
nodes.summary: In 2023, Alexion acquired and licensed Pfizer’s early-stage rare disease gene therapy assets for up to $1 billion: $300 million upfront, contingent milestones, and tiered sales royalties. Pfizer recorded a $222 million pretax gain. The text also describes agreements following Upjohn’s 2020 separation and combination with Mylan to form Viatris, covering transitional agency services, manufacturing under MSAs, tax and employee matters, and other arrangements. TSA services were largely completed by year-end 2023; agreement amounts were immaterial in 2022–2024. Net amounts payable to Viatris were $105 million at year-end 2024 versus $33 million in 2023, with related cash flows classified as operating activities.

nodes.title: C. Equity-Method Investments
nodes.summary: The notes describe Pfizer’s Haleon equity-method investment: its 2024 share sales, $945 million gain, reduction in ownership from 32% to about 15%, and transition after October from equity-method accounting to fair-value accounting because significant influence ended. They present the investment carrying-value rollforward, related adjustments, and Haleon summarized financial information. They also explain the Consumer Healthcare JV’s 2022 debt issuance, loans, dividends, repayments, and termination of Pfizer’s indemnity of GSK’s guarantees. Finally, they describe Pfizer’s 11.7% ViiV interest, suspended equity-method accounting since 2016 after its carrying value reached zero, dividends recognized as income, and summarized ViiV financial information.

nodes.title: D. Collaborative Arrangements
nodes.summary: Describes the company’s collaborative arrangements for marketed and developing medicines, including their varied co-development, research, manufacturing, and commercialization roles and risks. Details the 2021 Biohaven migraine-drug collaboration, its $500 million upfront and equity payments, $263 million expense recognition, and the 2022 acquisition of remaining Biohaven shares for about $11.5 billion. Summarizes 2022–2024 collaboration revenues and expenses by category, explains the drivers and nature of each category, and notes that the figures exclude third-party transactions and other product costs.

nodes.title: E. Research and Development Arrangement
key_items: Research and Development Funding Arrangement with Blackstone
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s Blackstone arrangement provides up to $550 million during 2023–2026 to co-fund specified treatment development costs, recognized as a reduction of R&D expense ($135 million in 2024; $175 million in 2023). Blackstone may receive up to $468 million in regulatory-approval milestones, up to $550 million in sales-based milestones, and mid-to-high-single-digit royalties; milestones are capitalized and amortized, while royalties are cost of sales. Pfizer describes its cost-realignment program (expected total $2.9 billion, primarily through 2025; $2.6 billion incurred by year-end 2024) and manufacturing-optimization program (first phase expected at $1.6 billion; $1.2 billion incurred). It reports 2022–2024 restructuring and acquisition-related costs, depreciation, implementation costs, and benefit credits, totaling $2.738 billion, $3.426 billion, and $2.018 billion, respectively, with explanations of major segment charges and acquisition-related expenses.

Covers Pfizer’s share-based compensation accounting and major acquisitions, including Seagen’s finalized purchase accounting and results and 2022 deals; the Alexion gene-therapy divestiture and post-Upjohn arrangements with Viatris; Haleon and ViiV equity-method investments and the Consumer Healthcare JV; collaboration activities, Biohaven payments and acquisition, and collaboration revenues and expenses; and the Blackstone R&D funding arrangement, restructuring and manufacturing-optimization programs, and related costs.

nodes.title: Cost Realignment and Manufacturing Optimization
key_items: A. Realigning our Cost Base Program
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s cost realignment program, launched in late 2023, is expected to cost about $2.9 billion through 2025, mainly for severance, exits, implementation, and asset write-downs; $2.6 billion had been incurred through 2024. Its manufacturing optimization program, launched in 2024, targets lower cost of goods through efficiencies, network changes, and portfolio enhancements. Phase one is expected to cost $1.6 billion, with $1.2 billion incurred by year-end 2024; most costs relate to Biopharma restructuring, with cash outlays mainly expected in 2025–2026.

nodes.title: C. Key Activities
nodes.summary: The section reports Pfizer’s 2022–2024 acquisition and cost-reduction/productivity costs: restructuring charges and credits by employee terminations, asset impairments and exit costs; transaction and integration costs; benefit credits; restructuring-related depreciation; implementation costs by income-statement category; and total costs. Notes explain program charges, acquisition-related service and integration expenses (including Seagen, Arena and GBT employee awards), and depreciation and implementation costs. It also summarizes restructuring accrual provisions, utilization, year-end balances, foreign-currency adjustments, and current/noncurrent liability classifications for 2023–2024.

summary: Pfizer’s section covers its consolidation, segments, acquisitions, accounting standards, estimates, fair-value methods, foreign-currency translation, and revenue recognition, including sales deductions, receivables, collaborations, and royalties. It explains inventory, operating and R&D expenses, long-lived assets, impairment, investments, derivatives, cash flows, taxes and contingencies, pensions, legal and environmental exposures, and share-based payments. It also reviews major acquisitions, divestitures, collaborations, cost-realignment and manufacturing-optimization programs, related charges, restructuring accruals, and costs from 2022–2024.

title: Note 4. Other (Income)/Deductions—Net
summary: Pfizer’s 2022–2024 other income/deductions, net, comprise interest, equity-security gains/losses, collaboration income, benefit costs, legal matters, impairments, Haleon equity-method results and other items. Notes explain capitalized interest and 2024 interest changes related to Seagen financing; investment gains/losses; legal expenses; annual intangible-asset impairments and their causes and assets; Haleon results; and other income, dividends, sales gains and charges. The disclosure also presents 2024 impaired-asset fair values and impairment amounts by asset type, and describes the discounted-cash-flow valuation method and its key estimates, including cash-flow forecasts, competitive and regulatory risks, trial success probabilities, discount and tax rates.

title: Note 5. Tax Matters

nodes.title: A. Taxes on Income from Continuing Operations
nodes.summary: The note reports pre-tax continuing-operations income or loss by U.S. and international location for 2022–2024 and explains year-over-year changes, including revenue, costs, restructuring, acquisition expenses, impairments, amortization, and equity-security results. It details current and deferred U.S. and international income-tax provisions or benefits, and explains effective-rate changes from jurisdictional earnings mix, tax resolutions, and the TCJA Transition Tax. Acquisition-related tax liabilities are excluded. The company’s $15 billion Transition Tax is payable over eight years through 2026; the sixth installment was paid in 2024, the seventh is due in 2025, and remaining amounts are classified as current or noncurrent. The note also introduces cash income taxes paid, net of refunds, by U.S. and international source.

nodes.title: B. Tax Rate Reconciliation
nodes.summary: The text reconciles Pfizer’s U.S. statutory 21% tax rate to effective rates for continuing operations in 2022–2024, showing impacts from non-U.S. taxation, Transition Tax, settlements, the Foreign-Derived Intangible Income deduction, state and local taxes, charitable contributions, R&D credits, interest, and other items. It notes that 2023 percentages were amplified by low pretax income. Explanations cover jurisdictional earnings mix, U.S. tax on foreign operations, uncertain tax positions, incentives in Singapore and Puerto Rico, 2022 R&D capitalization rules, state valuation allowances including Seagen, and routine business effects; related details are cross-referenced to Note 5A.

nodes.title: C. Deferred Taxes
nodes.summary: The text presents 2024 and 2023 deferred tax assets and liabilities by category, before jurisdictional netting, and explains key year-over-year movements, valuation allowances, carryforward adjustments for unrecognized tax benefits, balance-sheet classifications, and excluded tax attributes deemed unlikely to be used. It describes tax-loss, credit and contribution carryforwards, their expiration periods and Section 382 limits. It also notes $58.0 billion of indefinitely reinvested foreign earnings for which no U.S. tax provision was recorded, explains why the potential deferred liability cannot be practicably determined, and says estimates are regularly updated.

nodes.title: D. Tax Contingencies
key_items: Financial Assets and Liabilities Not Measured at Fair Value on a Recurring Basis
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes uncertain tax positions, reporting $2.0 billion in net unrecognized tax benefits and $2.5 billion in related assets at year-end 2024, with reconciliations, interest and penalties, audit status across U.S. and international jurisdictions, and possible benefit decreases of up to $200 million within 12 months. The text also presents tax effects on other comprehensive income and accumulated other comprehensive loss movements, then fair-value hierarchy tables for financial assets and liabilities, valuation methods and classifications, and carrying versus estimated fair values of debt and other instruments.

summary: Covers continuing-operations income by U.S. and international source, income-tax provisions and cash taxes, the Transition Tax and effective tax-rate reconciliation for 2022–2024. It details deferred tax assets and liabilities, valuation allowances, carryforwards, and indefinitely reinvested foreign earnings; uncertain tax positions, audits, interest and penalties, and tax effects in other comprehensive income. It also presents fair-value hierarchy information, valuation methods, and carrying and estimated fair values of financial instruments.

title: Short-term investments
summary: Pfizer Inc. and its subsidiary companies’ financial-statement notes present investment classifications and begin a summary of total short-term, long-term, and equity-method investments. Listed short-term categories are readily determinable fair-value equity securities, available-for-sale debt securities, and held-to-maturity debt securities, followed by a total. Long-term categories begin with the same three types plus private equity securities carried at cost; some entries reference notes (a) and (b). Amounts are stated in millions.

title: Total Long-term investments Equity-method investments (a)
key_items: E. Derivative Financial Instruments and Hedging Activities
summary: The notes detail investment balances and classifications, including Haleon and life-sciences investments; debt-security types, fair values, maturities, and immaterial expected credit losses; and equity-security realized and unrealized gains/losses and adjustments. They report short-term borrowings, commercial-paper rates, credit facilities and availability; long-term debt by maturity, carrying-value adjustments, and Seagen-related issuance. They also describe foreign-exchange and interest-rate risks, hedging methods and accounting treatment, and derivative fair values and notional amounts for 2024 and 2023.

title: Pfizer Inc.
summary: Pfizer explains accounting for foreign-exchange and interest-rate hedges, including fair-value, cash-flow and net-investment hedges, excluded amounts, and non-designated derivatives. title: Note 16. Contingencies and Certain Commitments
summary: Note 16 describes Pfizer’s ordinary-course contingencies and commitments, including legal matters, guarantees, indemnifications, and separately referenced tax contingencies. Legal risks include patent, product-liability, commercial, environmental, and government proceedings, potentially causing damages, royalties, fines, penalties, or criminal charges. Pfizer discusses litigation uncertainty, accruals for probable estimable losses, inability to estimate additional possible losses, estimation assumptions, environmental disclosure thresholds, and factors used to identify principal cases. Patent proceedings include challenges to Pfizer and partner patents, infringement claims, damages suits, and administrative reviews, with potential effects on sales and financial results. Examples include international Eliquis and Comirnaty challenges, pneumococcal vaccine patents, and U.S. plaintiff actions concerning generic Xeljanz and Mektovi, including settlements and ongoing suits.

title: Pfizer Patent Litigation: Xeljanz and Mektovi
summary: Pfizer describes patent disputes involving its and partners’ products, including generic challenges, damages claims, third-party infringement suits, and patent-review proceedings, which could affect sales or result in damages, royalties, or sales restrictions. For Xeljanz, several generic-manufacturer suits have settled; SpecGx and Breckenridge settled in November 2024, while an action against Alkem, filed in December 2024, remains. For Mektovi, Pfizer sued generic filers over six patents; one case settled in January 2025, and litigation against Teva over three patents continues.

title: Pfizer Drug Patent Litigation
summary: Pfizer reports generic-drug patent disputes: it sued ANDA filers over Vyndaqel/Vyndamax, Oxbryta, Nurtec, Xtandi and Inlyta, asserting patent validity and infringement; Oxbryta filers did not challenge composition or treatment patents. Separately, Pfizer and BioNTech face Comirnaty infringement claims from Alnylam, Moderna, Arbutus/Genevant, GSK and Promosome in U.S. and international courts, seeking unspecified damages. Proceedings include patent reviews and rulings, including European patent revocations and invalidity findings, alongside a U.K. finding that one patent was valid and infringed.

key_items: Matters Involving Pfizer and its Collaboration/Licensing Partners Comirnaty (tozinameran)
summary: The page details Pfizer’s legal matters: Enanta’s Paxlovid patent case ended with the patent ruled invalid; GSK alleges Abrysvo infringes seven U.S. patents and seeks damages and an injunction, while a U.K. court invalidated two GSK patents. CureVac disputes concern Comirnaty patents in the U.S. and U.K., where two patents were ruled invalid. Product litigation covers asbestos exposure claims, a settled West Virginia Lipitor generic-delay action, and Docetaxel hair-loss and blocked-tear-duct lawsuits consolidated in federal multidistrict proceedings.

title: Zantac
summary: Pfizer reports Zantac cancer lawsuits in U.S., Canada, and Israel-related jurisdictions, including personal-injury, consumer, and medical-monitoring claims. A federal MDL court excluded plaintiffs’ experts and granted summary judgment on causation in 2022, dismissing the complaints; appeals are pending. Many state cases remain, though most involving alleged use of Pfizer products were settled or covered by settlement agreements by January 2025. Chantix recall-related economic-loss class actions are coordinated in a New York MDL; an Israeli class action was dismissed. Depo-Provera/MPA meningioma suits were consolidated in a Florida MDL in February 2025. The text also describes Monsanto-related indemnities assumed by spun-off companies, now Bayer’s subsidiary, and Pfizer’s assumed Wyeth environmental remediation obligations at Bound Brook, plus other remediation proceedings.

title: Pfizer Legal Proceedings and Environmental Matters
summary: The page reviews litigation involving Zantac, including federal dismissals under appeal, Canadian and U.S. state actions, and settlements covering most state cases involving Pfizer products. It explains New Monsanto’s and Solutia’s indemnification and defense of Pharmacia for former agricultural and chemical business liabilities, including environmental claims. Their descriptions are summaries qualified by Pfizer’s restated certificate of incorporation and bylaws, and by the base and ninth supplemental indentures, respectively, incorporated into the related Form 10-K. title: DESCRIPTION OF CAPITAL STOCK
key_items: Anti-takeover Effects of the Certificate of Incorporation, Bylaws and Delaware Law
summary: Pfizer may issue 12 billion common shares ($0.05 par) and 27 million no-par preferred shares. Common stock has one vote per share, no redemption, conversion, call, or preemptive rights, and provides for declared dividends and equal, ratable liquidation distributions; outstanding shares are fully paid and nonassessable, and trade as PFE on the NYSE. The Board sets preferred-stock series and their terms. Charter and bylaws may deter control changes through limits on special-meeting calls, board authority over preferred stock, rights, board size and vacancies, and written stockholder action. Delaware DGCL Section 203 generally restricts business combinations with 15%-or-more interested stockholders for three years, subject to specified board, ownership, or stockholder-approval exceptions, potentially delaying or discouraging takeovers and depressing share price.

title: DESCRIPTION OF DEBT SECURITIES

nodes.title: Euro Notes: Principal, Interest and Payments
nodes.summary: The page explains that the notes are governed by Pfizer’s base indenture and ninth supplemental indenture, which define holders’ rights. The €750 million notes mature March 6, 2027, were issued in specified denominations, and bear 1% annual interest payable each March 6 using ACTUAL/ACTUAL (ICMA); record holders are determined 15 calendar days beforehand. The London branch of Bank of New York Mellon is paying agent, with payments routed through Euroclear and/or Clearstream. Payments are in euros, but may switch to U.S. dollars if euros become unavailable or cease to be used, at Pfizer’s determined exchange rate; this is not a default, and the trustee and agent have no exchange-conversion duties.

nodes.title: Payment of Additional Amounts
nodes.summary: Pfizer generally pays note amounts without U.S. tax withholding, but gross-ups eligible non-U.S. beneficial owners when withholding is legally required, subject to exceptions covering U.S.-connected holders, intermediary or entity status, specified tax classifications, noncompliance with documentation rules, non-withholding taxes, certain tax types, available EU paying agents, late legal changes or presentment, FATCA, and combinations thereof. Pfizer otherwise assumes no tax liability. The text defines “United States” and “United States person.” The unsecured, unsubordinated notes rank equally with Pfizer’s other such debt, are listed on the NYSE without a listing-maintenance commitment, and are subject to limited merger and substantially-all-assets transfer restrictions. The indenture has no other restrictive covenants or specified protections found in certain other Pfizer notes.

nodes.title: Additional Amounts, Ranking and Listing
nodes.summary: The text lists tax-related exceptions to Pfizer’s obligation to pay additional amounts, including specified holder statuses, reporting failures, non-withholding taxes, certain taxes, alternative paying-agent availability, late legal changes or note presentation, FATCA withholding, and combinations thereof. It disclaims other governmental tax payments and defines “United States” and “United States person.” The notes are unsecured, unsubordinated obligations ranking equally with Pfizer’s other such debt, and are listed on the NYSE, which Pfizer need not maintain and may discontinue at any time.

nodes.title: Covenants
nodes.summary: The indenture restricts Pfizer from merging or consolidating, or transferring substantially all its assets, but permits other transfers. It otherwise lacks protective covenants, including protections for leveraged transactions and covenants on debt, coverage, repurchases, dividends, acquisitions, liens, subsidiary guarantees, and sale-leasebacks. Pfizer may issue additional notes without holder consent on substantially identical terms as a single series, provided no default exists and the notes are fungible for U.S. federal tax purposes.

nodes.title: Optional Redemption of Notes; Redemption for Tax Reasons; No Sinking Fund
nodes.summary: The issuer may redeem notes before December 6, 2026, at the greater of par or the present value of remaining principal and interest discounted at the Comparable Government Bond Rate plus 15 basis points, plus accrued interest; from that date onward, redemption is at par plus accrued interest. Scheduled interest remains payable to holders of record, and prices use an actual-days/365- or 366-day basis. Redemption notice must be mailed 10–60 days ahead; after notice, called notes become due, and interest stops accruing after redemption unless payment defaults. The issuer must fund payment by the redemption date. Partial redemptions are selected by Euroclear/Clearstream for global notes or the trustee otherwise. The text defines Comparable Government Bond, its rate, Independent Investment Banker, and Reference Treasury Dealers, and states there is no sinking fund.

nodes.title: Redemption for Tax Reasons
nodes.summary: The issuer may redeem an entire applicable series of notes, but not part of a series, if a U.S. law, regulation, ruling, or official interpretive position changes or is amended on or after February 28, 2017, causing or, based on an opinion from recognized independent tax counsel selected by the issuer, expected to cause additional tax-related payments. The issuer must give holders 10–60 days’ prior notice and pay 100% of principal plus accrued unpaid interest and any additional amounts through, but excluding, the redemption date.

The text describes each system’s services, governance, access, settlement and distribution procedures, and disclaims responsibility for beneficial-ownership records and payments. It covers inter-system arrangements, limits on pledging interests without certificates, secondary trading and possible business-day/time-zone delays, and conditions for exchanging global notes for definitive certificates, including denominations and payment and transfer procedures.

nodes.title: Modification of Indenture
nodes.summary: A supplemental indenture may generally modify noteholders’ rights with consent from holders of a majority in aggregate principal amount of all affected outstanding series, voting as one class. However, changes to maturity, principal or interest payments, payment currency, enforcement rights at maturity, conversion rights, required consent percentages, or provisions governing waivers of defaults or covenants cannot bind a holder without that holder’s consent.

nodes.title: Events of Default
nodes.summary: Events of default include missed principal or premium payments, sinking-fund payments overdue 60 days, interest overdue 60 days, uncured covenant breaches after 90 days’ written notice, and specified bankruptcy or insolvency actions. Defaults on other debt or one note series do not automatically affect another; the trustee may withhold notice of nonpayment defaults if it believes doing so benefits holders. For a continuing default, the trustee or holders of at least 33% of a series may accelerate payment. A majority may rescind acceleration subject to stated payment, timing, and cure or waiver conditions. A majority of affected series may waive past defaults, except payment defaults and protected covenants. Trustee action generally requires reasonable indemnity; a series majority may direct proceedings or remedies subject to limitations. The issuer must provide the trustee an annual certificate reporting any indenture defaults and their status.

nodes.title: Defeasance
nodes.summary: Defeasance means discharge from some or all obligations under the indenture. Subject to conditions, an irrevocable deposit with the trustee of enough cash or government securities to cover a series’ principal, interest, premium, and other sums through maturity or redemption allows the issuer to choose either full discharge for that series or release from specified restrictive covenants and certain events of default. The issuer must provide the trustee an officer’s certificate and legal opinion confirming all conditions precedent are met.

title: Insider Trading Policy and Purpose
key_items: CORPORATE POLICY 604A: PROHIBITION ON INSIDER TRADING
summary: Exhibit 19 presents Pfizer Corporate Policy 604A, version 2.0, including its effective and update dates, sponsoring Legal Division, and Contact Email heading. The policy covers trading in Pfizer securities or those of business-related public companies while possessing relevant material nonpublic information (MNPI), and Pfizer’s own securities transactions and repurchase plans. It outlines how materiality and public dissemination are assessed, notes that information materiality can differ between companies, and refers readers to the glossary and Policy 401 on safeguarding sensitive information. It explains legal penalties for insider trading and states that the policy supports, but does not replace, each individual’s responsibility to comply with the law.

title: Scope
summary: The Policy applies globally to colleagues, directors, contracted resources, and defined affiliated persons, including spouses, minor children, household members, dependents, and controlled entities. Trading includes gifts of securities, including estate-planning gifts to trusts, and charitable donations. Suspected violations involving Pfizer or other company securities must be reported immediately under the Blue Book and Corporate Policy 201; reporting channels may vary by market and privacy laws. Policy questions go to the Corporate Governance Department. Noncompliance may result in discipline, including termination.

title: Guiding Principles
summary: Insiders must act with integrity, keep material nonpublic information (MNPI) confidential, and trade in Pfizer or other relevant companies’ securities only as permitted by policy, including Corporate Policy 604B on MNPI and Regulation Fair Disclosure. Trades must have a legitimate purpose and generally occur only when the insider has no MNPI and is not subject to a blackout. Covered Persons must also trade only during Open Window Periods and obtain pre-clearance. Information is considered public only after one full trading day has elapsed following disclosure.

title: Policy
key_items: Prohibition on Transacting in Securities While in Possession of Material Nonpublic Information
Prohibited Transactions; Permitted Transactions; Event-Specific Restricted Trading Periods (Special Blackouts); Post-Termination Trading
summary: Pfizer’s policy prohibits Insiders with material nonpublic information (MNPI) from trading Pfizer securities or relevant other-company securities when the information was obtained through Pfizer work, advising others to trade, or tipping others. It covers all Pfizer securities, derivatives, and gifts; requires confidentiality and restricts disclosure except as authorized under cited policies. While aware of Pfizer MNPI, prohibited transactions include buying or selling shares, certain stock-plan transfers or contribution changes, voluntary investment-program changes, and hedging. Permitted activities include cash option exercises when shares are retained, unchanged periodic plan contributions and matching, and previously elected dividend reinvestment. Special blackouts may restrict trading and must remain confidential; MNPI still bars trading without a blackout notice. Former Insiders must wait to trade until MNPI becomes public or immaterial.

title: Covered Persons’ Trading Requirements
summary: Covered Persons must trade only during Open Window Periods and obtain advance pre-clearance from the Corporate Secretary or designee for every Pfizer securities transaction, whether or not they possess MNPI or trade during an open window. Quarterly blackouts begin two weeks before each fiscal quarter ends and continue through a full trading day after results are publicly disclosed; notice is customary but not required for restrictions to apply. Open windows do not permit trading while possessing MNPI or subject to a special blackout, except under a qualifying SEC Rule 10b5-1 plan consistent with Pfizer policy.

title: PFIZER POLICY RELATING TO RULE 10b5-1 TRADING PLANS

nodes.title: Restrictions Related to Each Plan
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s policy applies to Rule 10b5-1 plans between employees or directors and a service provider. Plan establishment requires no trading blackout or material nonpublic information and prior corporate-secretary preclearance; trades must wait 90 days plus the specified filing-based period (capped at 120 days) for directors and Section 16 officers, or 60 days for others. Modifications require no blackout or inside information and restart the applicable waiting period; terminations require preclearance. Participants generally may have only one plan at a time, with exceptions for eligible tax-withholding sell-to-cover plans and a later-starting plan subject to waiting-period rules. No more than one single-transaction plan is allowed per 12 months, except sell-to-cover plans. Participants may not make same-direction transactions outside an active plan, except under specified Pfizer savings plans. Directors and Section 16 officers retain their Exchange Act duties and liabilities, should consult counsel, and must cooperate with Pfizer’s SEC reporting.

nodes.title: EXHIBIT 97
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s policy, adopted under Dodd-Frank and SEC/NYSE rules, defines covered executives, incentive compensation, financial measures, restatements, lookback periods, and related terms. After a qualifying restatement, excess pre-tax compensation received in the prior three fiscal years (plus eligible transition periods) must be forfeited or repaid, subject to narrow impracticability exceptions. The policy sets repayment methods and deadlines, prohibits indemnification, and addresses administration, amendments, legal compliance, other recovery rights, termination, and binding effect on successors and representatives.
